title: Episode 221: Italy: The Risorgimento: Giuseppe Garibaldi, the Thousand Redshirts, and United Italy
description:
In 1815, Austrian statesman Prince Metternich famously dismissed Italy as nothing more than a 'geographical expression'—a fragmented peninsula parcelled out among Austrian overlords, the Papal States, and the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Yet out of this foreign subjugation arose the 'Risorgimento'—the Resurgence—an epic romantic crusade to forge an independent, united Italian nation. Driven by three visionary figures—Giuseppe Mazzini, the prophet of democratic republicanism; Count Camillo di Cavour, the brilliant diplomatic prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia; and Giuseppe Garibaldi, the charismatic swashbuckling guerrilla hero of the redshirts. In May 1860, with only a thousand volunteer fighters armed with obsolete muskets, Garibaldi sailed from Genoa to Sicily, routing royal Bourbon armies, liberating Naples, and handing over an entire southern kingdom to King Victor Emmanuel II at the historic meeting of Teano. Discover the passion, battlefield daring, and unification of modern Italy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of Italy with the heroic nineteenth-century struggle for national independence: The Risorgimento. In a whirlwind campaign of romantic daring, a thousand volunteers in red shirts united a peninsula that had been divided since the fall of Rome. Here is George with the story of Giuseppe Garibaldi and the birth of modern Italy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'A GEOGRAPHICAL EXPRESSION': FRACTURED ITALY
Following the defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815, the Congress of Vienna restored the ancient feudal divisions of the Italian peninsula. Northern Italy—the wealthy provinces of Lombardy and Venetia—was occupied directly by the Austrian Habsburg Empire; the center was ruled by the conservative temporal authority of the Pope in the Papal States; the south and Sicily were governed by the reactionary Spanish Bourbon Dynasty in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies; and independent Italian rule survived only in the northwestern Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia under the House of Savoy. Austrian Chancellor Prince Metternich arrogantly remarked that 'Italy is only a geographical expression'—a region with no political unity or common destiny. Italians had no shared currency, no national parliament, and spoke regional dialects so distinct that a Sicilian could not understand a Venetian. Secret revolutionary societies like the 'Carbonari'—the Charcoal Burners—plotted underground rebellions in candlelit cellars, dreaming of liberty, but their early uprisings in 1820 and 1831 were ruthlessly crushed by Austrian bayonets.  In 1815, following the defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna partitioned the Italian peninsula into eight autocratic states under Austrian military domination, prompting Austrian Prince Metternich to dismiss Italy with cold disdain as merely 'a geographical expression'. But beneath the surface of reactionary police states, secret patriotic societies like the Carbonari whispered dreams of freedom, unity, and a revived Roman republic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE PROPHET AND THE POLITICIAN: MAZZINI AND CAVOUR
The intellectual soul of the Risorgimento was Giuseppe Mazzini, a passionate Genoese lawyer who founded the revolutionary movement 'Young Italy' in 1831. Mazzini was the prophet of Italian nationalism, preaching that Italian unification was a sacred moral duty and divine mission that could only be achieved through a popular, democratic republican uprising of the people. Exiled across Europe, Mazzini inspired a generation of young Italian patriots with his rallying cry: 'Dio e Popolo'—God and the People. In contrast to Mazzini's romantic idealism stood the pragmatic diplomatic mastermind of the movement: Count Camillo di Cavour, the prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia. A wealthy aristocrat and disciple of British liberalism, Cavour modernized the Piedmontese economy with railways, telegraphs, and free trade. Recognizing that Italy could never expel the mighty Austrian army through romantic volunteer revolts alone, Cavour entered the Crimean War alongside Britain and France to put the Italian Question on the European diplomatic agenda, securing a secret military alliance with French Emperor Napoleon III in 1858.  The Italian unification—the Risorgimento—was forged by the complementary genius of contrasting leaders: Giuseppe Mazzini, the fiery moral prophet who founded Young Italy from exile and inspired the youth to sacrifice their lives for a republic, and Count Camillo di Cavour, the brilliant, bespectacled Prime Minister of Piedmont-Sardinia who wielded rail networks, free trade, and calculated European diplomacy to expel Austria from northern Italy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE HERO OF TWO WORLDS: GIUSEPPE GARIBALDI
If Mazzini was the soul of the Risorgimento and Cavour the brain, the sword was Giuseppe Garibaldi. Born in Nice in 1807, Garibaldi was a professional sea captain who joined Mazzini's Young Italy and was sentenced to death for mutiny in 1834. Fleeing to South America, Garibaldi spent twelve swashbuckling years as a guerrilla commander fighting for freedom in the civil wars of Brazil and Uruguay. Leading the Italian Legion in Montevideo, Garibaldi adopted the signature uniform that would become immortal in European history: loose, bright red wool tunics—originally manufactured for slaughterhouse workers in Argentina—along with a poncho and a flowing black silk neckerchief. Returning to Italy during the revolutions of 1848, Garibaldi defended the short-lived Roman Republic against French armies, holding the Janiculum Hill with epic heroism before leading his retreating fighters across the Apennine Mountains, losing his beloved Brazilian wife Anita in the marshes of Ravenna. By 1860, the 'Hero of Two Worlds' was living as a simple farmer on the rocky island of Caprera off Sardinia.  The charismatic warrior-hero of the movement was Giuseppe Garibaldi: sea captain, guerrilla leader, and fearless champion of freedom who had fought for republics in Brazil and Uruguay before returning to Italy. Wearing his iconic red poncho, broad-brimmed gaucho hat, and cavalry saber, Garibaldi possessed a magnetic personal courage that inspired ordinary workers, students, and peasants to follow him through bullets, starvation, and exile.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE EXPEDITION OF THE THOUSAND: SICILY 1860
In April 1860, a popular insurrection broke out against the oppressive Bourbon regime in Palermo, Sicily. Garibaldi saw his moment: against Cavour's cautious advice, Garibaldi gathered a volunteer force of one thousand and eighty-eight civilian patriots in Genoa—consisting of university students, lawyers, doctors, poets, and veteran revolutionaries, accompanied by a solitary woman, Rose Montmasson. Known to history as 'The Thousand' or 'The Redshirts,' they commandeered two dilapidated paddle-steamers, the Piemonte and the Lombardo, armed with obsolete flintlock muskets and minimal ammunition. On May 11, 1860, under the protective cover of two neutral British warships anchored in the bay, Garibaldi landed at Marsala on the western tip of Sicily. Four days later, at the Battle of Calatafimi, Garibaldi's Thousand confronted three thousand regular Bourbon troops armed with modern rifles atop a steep terraced hill. When his commander Nino Bixio suggested retreat, Garibaldi uttered his immortal resolve: 'Here we make Italy, or we die!' Charging uphill with fixed bayonets, the Redshirts routed the royal forces, sending shockwaves across Europe.  In May 1860, hearing of a popular uprising in Sicily against the Bourbon monarchy, Garibaldi embarked on the most audacious military gamble in modern history: the Expedition of the Thousand. Sailing secretly from Genoa aboard two battered steamships with one thousand volunteer Redshirts armed with antiquated muskets and barely any ammunition, Garibaldi landed at Marsala, declaring himself dictator of Sicily in the name of King Victor Emmanuel.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CAPTURE OF PALERMO AND THE MARCH ON NAPLES
Joined by thousands of Sicilian peasants armed with scythes and hunting rifles, Garibaldi marched across the rugged mountains to the capital city of Palermo, defended by twenty thousand regular Bourbon soldiers with heavy artillery. Using audacity and urban guerrilla tactics, Garibaldi infiltrated the city through the Porta Termini at dawn on May 27, throwing up hundreds of barricades in the narrow streets. For three days, as royal warships shelled the city, the citizens of Palermo fought beside the Redshirts. Astonishingly, the Bourbon general lost his nerve and signed an armistice, evacuating twenty thousand troops by sea. Proclaiming himself Dictator of Sicily in the name of King Victor Emmanuel II, Garibaldi crossed the Strait of Messina onto the Italian mainland in August. His advance through Calabria was a triumphal procession: Bourbon garrisons surrendered without firing a shot, their soldiers defecting to the liberator. On September 7, 1860, arriving ahead of his troops on a regular railway train, Garibaldi rode into the royal capital of Naples in an open carriage, greeted by half a million ecstatic citizens chanting his name.  At the Battle of Calatafimi, facing superior royal troops entrenched on a terraced hillside, Garibaldi famously shouted to his second-in-command: 'Here we make Italy, or we die!' Charging uphill with fixed bayonets, the Redshirts routed the Bourbon forces, seized the island capital of Palermo through street-by-street fighting, crossed the Strait of Messina onto the mainland, and entered Naples in triumph as the Bourbon king fled in panic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MEETING AT TEANO: THE GIFT OF A KINGDOM
Garibaldi's lightning triumph created a moment of extreme geopolitical peril for Cavour. Cavour feared that Garibaldi, encouraged by republicans like Mazzini, would march north into Rome, provoking French and Austrian military intervention to defend the Pope, which could destroy everything. Acting with ruthless speed, Cavour dispatched King Victor Emmanuel II with the regular Piedmontese army marching south through the Papal States to intercept the Redshirts. On the crisp autumn morning of October 26, 1860, near the rural town of Teano in Campania, the two armies met along the highway. Riding out on a modest pony, dressed in his worn red shirt, grey poncho, and round cap, Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel mounted on a magnificent thoroughbred in full royal military regalia. Garibaldi raised his hat, extended his hand, and shouted in a clear voice: 'Saluto il primo Re d'Italia!'—I salute the first King of Italy! In an act of supreme patriotic selflessness, Garibaldi surrendered the entire conquered Kingdom of the Two Sicilies to the crown. Refusing all titles, estates, and gold offered by the King, Garibaldi asked only for a bag of seed corn for his farm on Caprera, boarding a ship for home the next day.  With southern Italy liberated, radical republicans urged Garibaldi to march on Rome and declare a republic, which would have triggered catastrophic war with Catholic France. Instead, on October 26, 1860, at the village crossroads of Teano, Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel II, saluted the monarch as 'King of Italy', and selflessly surrendered his conquests, asking for no titles or wealth before sailing home to his rocky island of Caprera with only a sack of dried beans and seed corn.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PROCLAMATION OF ROME: CAPITAL OF ITALY: 1870
On March 17, 1861, the newly assembled national Italian parliament in Turin formally proclaimed the unified Kingdom of Italy, with Victor Emmanuel II as its first constitutional monarch. Yet the Risorgimento remained incomplete: Venetia remained under Austrian rule, and Rome was garrisoned by French troops protecting Pope Pius IX. In 1866, allying with Bismarck's Prussia in the Austro-Prussian War, Italy annexed Venice. Finally, in September 1870, when the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War forced Napoleon III to withdraw the French garrison from Rome, Italian troops seized the opportunity. On September 20, 1870, Italian royal artillery blasted a breach through the ancient Aurelian walls at the Porta Pia. Italian bersaglieri infantry poured through the breach to the cheers of the Roman populace. The temporal rule of the Popes, which had endured for over a thousand years, was brought to an end, with the Pope retreating into the Vatican as a self-proclaimed 'prisoner.' In July 1871, Rome was officially inaugurated as the eternal capital of a united Italy, fulfilling the centuries-old dream of the Risorgimento.  In March 1861, the first unified Italian Parliament proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy, and nine years later, in September 1870, Italian troops breached the Aurelian Walls at the Porta Pia, annexing Rome and proclaiming the Eternal City as the capital of a united nation. The Risorgimento fulfilled centuries of patriotic longing, uniting an ancient cultural heartland into a modern, sovereign nation dedicated to freedom and national self-determination.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
From the redshirts of Garibaldi to the breach at Porta Pia, Italy was reborn as a modern unified nation, uniting the artistic legacy of the Renaissance with the fire of national freedom. Next week, we continue our Major European Nations Series with Episode 222: Russia Part 1: Peter the Great, the Window to the West, and the Foundation of Saint Petersburg. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
